transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-18
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood Eng), Leon Torres (Sapphire CTO), Aisha Patel (Sapphire ML Eng), Rajiv Menon (Sapphire Infra)

Summary: quick sync on the pilot latency behavior, specifically TTFT spikes we saw after increasing target sequence length; decide micro-benchmark matrix and owner for kernel decisions.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, i know this is end of week so we keep tight. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Leon Torres: yep leon here, aisha and rajiv are on my side.
[00:08] Aisha Patel: hi, aisha here.
[00:10] Rajiv Menon: rajiv on infra.
[00:12] Maya Chen: awesome, jordan from our side?
[00:15] Jordan Lee: jordan here, i'll own the kernel bit.
[00:17] Priya Kapoor: priya here for any runtime questions.
[00:20] Maya Chen: cool — quick context: last week we bumped default seq target from 128 to 256 to match your production path and saw TTFT regressions on streaming path, plus some jitter in sustained throughput. Wanted to go through the numbers, possible root causes and pick the micro-bench matrix.

[02:10] Jordan Lee: right, we ran the 500-sample run and saw TTFT median go from ~85ms to ~140ms with int8 kernels on our hosted nodes when seq increased. Notably the first token is picking a fallback kernel in a few percent of requests — looks like the kernel selector misclassed the early token shape.
[02:35] Aisha Patel: when you say "fallback" is that the rectangular-optimized kernel vs the fused attention kernel? we saw something like that in logs but the names were messy.
[02:45] Jordan Lee: yes exactly — the selector prefers the low-latency fused kernel for short sequences; when sequence prediction indicates a long run, it sometimes swaps and that swap in runtime triggers a higher TTFT. transcription sometimes shows "fused" as "fuse" or "fidded" so ignore that in the auto logs.
[03:05] Rajiv Menon: is that swap happening mid-request or before tokens start? our guess is mid-request due to prefetch heuristics.
[03:12] Jordan Lee: we're seeing both. In ~60% of the problematic traces it's pre-start decision, but ~40% show a micro swap after the KV cache warms and the runtime re-evaluates kernel choice. That recompile/reslection is cheap but impacts that first token.

[05:30] Leon Torres: from our side, the thing that matters is perceived latency to users. if first token is 2x worse that's painful. we can maybe accept slightly lower throughput but need consistent first-byte.
[05:45] Maya Chen: got it. two axes then: prevent kernel swap at runtime for the first request path, and improve KV cache warmup to give the runtime correct signals earlier.
[06:00] Jordan Lee: for kernel swap: we can pin the kernel for the initial blocks based on a lightweight sequence-length predictor that runs on the client prompt before scheduling. the overhead is minimal. We can also add a hysteresis window so the runtime won't flip kernels until after N tokens.
[06:30] Aisha Patel: hysteresis sounds promising. how invasive is that change? timeline?
[06:40] Jordan Lee: it's a runtime param — non-breaking, we can toggle it per-model in the pilot. i'd like to try hysteresis=8 tokens first.
[07:00] Priya Kapoor: also worth noting the KV cache prefix caching: your workload has many repeated prefixes, so if we prepopulate cache with those for the session it reduces the need to rescan and leads to better early-token probs. The auto-cacher sometimes mislabels tokens due to punctuation differences — the transcription reads KV as "K V" and sometimes "KV cash" in our logs, so scrubbing is needed.
[07:30] Rajiv Menon: we can provide top-50 prefixes and a sample of prompts. any privacy concerns we should be aware of? we'll anonymize.
[07:40] Maya Chen: perfect. next: benchmarking matrix — what exact runs should we schedule?
[08:10] Jordan Lee: propose: 1k requests per vector of config; configs = seq 128/256/512, kernels = Fused-FP32, Fused-INT8, Rectangular-FP32, Rectangular-INT8; streaming chunk sizes = 64/128; and toggle hysteresis param 0/8. Collect TTFT median/95th, token throughput, KV hit-rate and cold-start counts. Also measure memory and GPU util so we can show cost delta.
[09:00] Aisha Patel: that's a lot, but sane. do you need us to stand up any special env?
[09:08] Jordan Lee: for hosted we can run it; if you want dedicated parity we can mirror on your dedicated nodes with same image. For now let's run hosted + one dedicated node to compare.
[09:25] Leon Torres: cost numbers will matter — can you show cost-per-1M tokens under each kernel?
[09:30] Maya Chen: yes we'll include per-token cost delta in the spreadsheet.
[09:35] Rajiv Menon: curious about streaming chunking: in our app we often stream every 32 tokens. is chunk size 64 going to increase TTFT?
[09:45] Jordan Lee: streaming chunk math interacts with the scheduler — smaller chunks mean more RPCs and slightly higher per-token overhead but lower perceived latency for users seeing partial results. For TTFT the chunk size only matters if the scheduler defers the first chunk while waiting to accumulate more tokens; our streaming default tries to emit asap, but micro batching can introduce wait. We'll capture the per-chunk wait time in the traces.
[11:00] Aisha Patel: one anomaly — in a few pilot logs we saw a 400ms TTFT with low GPU util. any idea?
[11:15] Priya Kapoor: that smells like a network hiccup or retry from the load balancer; we traced one instance to our client side re-auth attempt — it looks like SSO token refresh was blocking in your platform for that request, so it wasn't the runtime.
[11:35] Leon Torres: ok we'll audit client refresh path.
[11:40] Maya Chen: good catch.
[12:05] Jordan Lee: on the kernel selector itself, we have heuristics that choose based on predicted remaining length and current sequence; given your workload mix (we need the histogram) we might prefer a fixed-policy pin for short TTL sessions. The fallback to rectangular is sometimes cheaper in throughput but worse for latency.
[13:00] Rajiv Menon: any risks to pinning?
[13:05] Jordan Lee: main risk is throughput degradation on long-run chats; pinning fused for everything will slightly reduce sustained throughput on long tails. tradeoff is consistent TTFT vs cost.
[13:20] Maya Chen: that's basically the business question — what do you value more? leon: consistent first token or max throughput?
[13:25] Leon Torres: consistent first token. we'll take a small cost increase if it fixes jitters.
[13:30] Maya Chen: copy. so plan: run the matrix but prioritize configs that favor consistent TTFT (hysteresis and pinned kernel), gather cost delta.
[14:00] Aisha Patel: about KV cache warmup: is there an easy toggle to prepopulate from session metadata?
[14:10] Jordan Lee: yes, we support prefix prewarm via a session hint. we'll prototype a script to call the prewarm endpoint with your top prefixes before session start. That should cut cold-hit TTFT.
[14:30] Rajiv Menon: we'll need an API key for that?
[14:35] Maya Chen: use the pilot API key; we'll generate a scoped prewarm token for you.
[14:45] Priya Kapoor: logging note — please enable debug tracing for 48 hours on these runs so we can capture kernel selection traces. It adds noise but very helpful.
[15:00] Leon Torres: agreed.
[15:10] Maya Chen: ok last part: timeline and owners recap.
[15:20] Jordan Lee: I'll run the hosted micro-benchmarks across the matrix and post results. If anything weird shows up I'll flag it for follow-up.
[15:30] Maya Chen: i'll package the baseline pricing numbers and the delta for pinned vs adaptive kernels.
[15:35] Aisha Patel: i'll send the sequence histogram and prompt samples today.
[15:40] Rajiv Menon: i'll confirm egress and region by Monday.
[15:45] Maya Chen: great. any other blockers?
[15:50] Leon Torres: none from me. thanks all.
[15:55] Maya Chen: thanks, we'll share the spreadsheet and set the kernel-deep-dive for 2025-12-22.

End of transcript.

Notes: several transcription artifacts present ("K V" vs "KV", "fused" sometimes transcribed as "fused"/"fussed"), some speaker label drift in auto-tool — validated by AE/SE post-call.
